definition: The original IETF standard defining TLS version 1.3, published August 2018. TLS 1.3 removed legacy cipher suites, mandated forward secrecy, and reduced the handshake to 1 round-trip. Obsoleted by RFC 9846 (July 2026), which re-specifies TLS 1.3 under the same version number.
technicalNote: TLS 1.3 is the foundation for PQC key exchange integration. RFC 8446 (now RFC 9846) defines the "key_share" extension that hybrid PQC groups (e.g., X25519MLKEM768) plug into without protocol changes.

definition: The NIST standard defining ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism), published August 2024.
The NIST standard defining ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), published August 2024.
The NIST standard defining SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), published August 2024.
The U.S. government standard for validating cryptographic modules. Hardware and software must pass FIPS 140-3 testing to be used in federal systems.
NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0, mandating PQC adoption timelines for national security systems.
An international standard (ISO/IEC 15408) for evaluating the security properties of IT products, used globally for government procurement.
technicalNote: The Common Criteria Recognition Arrangement (CCRA) is an arrangement between government participants: national Certification Bodies (e.g., BSI for Germany, ANSSI for France, NIAP for the US) authorise CC certificates, and other participants plan to recognise them within the arrangement's scope (collaborative Protection Profiles, or assurance up to EAL 2). Recognition is not an endorsement or guarantee of a product. EUCC is a separate EU scheme based on the Common Criteria, adopted under the Cybersecurity Act.

definition: EU Cybersecurity Certification Scheme — the European Union's harmonized product security certification scheme based on Common Criteria, adopted by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/482 under the EU Cybersecurity Act (2019).
technicalNote: A European cybersecurity certificate is recognised in all Member States under the Cybersecurity Act, but certification is voluntary unless Union or national law requires it. EUCC certificates at assurance level 'substantial' or 'high' are issued by accredited certification bodies (for 'high', authorised by the national cybersecurity certification authority) after evaluation by an ITSEF. The Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms document of the European Cybersecurity Certification Group gives recommendations on cryptographic mechanisms preferably used in products submitted to certification; it is maintained by an ECCG subgroup and is not a list of approved PQC algorithms.

definition: The EU regulation establishing a framework for electronic identification and trust services, including the European Digital Identity Wallet.

The EU Network and Information Security Directive 2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555). Article 21 requires essential and important entities to take appropriate and proportionate cybersecurity risk-management measures, including policies and procedures on the use of cryptography and, where appropriate, encryption. Member States had to adopt national measures by 17 October 2024 and apply them from 18 October 2024; what applies to a given entity depends on national law.
technicalNote: Article 21(2)(h) names cryptography and encryption policies as one of the minimum elements of the measures; the Directive text does not mention post-quantum cryptography. EU-level PQC timelines come from separate documents: the Commission's Recommendation of 11 April 2024 and the roadmap that EU Member States, supported by the Commission, issued in June 2025, which the Commission describes as a high-level paper aimed at Member States.

definition: A file format for storing a private key together with its X.509 certificate, commonly used for importing/exporting credentials.

The planned NIST standard for FN-DSA (FFT over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, based on Falcon). FIPS 206 is still in development; NIST has not published an Initial Public Draft or final standard.
The NIST Digital Signature Standard defining RSA, ECDSA, and EdDSA. Being deprecated in favor of PQC signature algorithms per NIST IR 8547.

NIST Internal Report setting the PQC transition timeline: quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards after 2035. Final since 27 October 2026; it replaced the initial public draft of 12 November 2024.
technicalNote: Covers RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA, finite-field and elliptic-curve DH and MQV at every key size of 112 bits of security or more. It recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default ML-KEM parameter set and allows a hybrid key-establishment scheme to be FIPS 140-validated when one input is approved.

definition: NIST Special Publication providing guidance on transitioning the use of cryptographic algorithms and key lengths. Defines which algorithms are approved, deprecated, or disallowed for federal use.
technicalNote: The current final edition is Revision 2 (March 2019); among other things it disallows SHA-1 for digital signature generation except where NIST protocol-specific guidance allows it. Revision 3 has been released only as an initial public draft (October 2024). NIST IR 8547 (October 2026) states that NIST will revise SP 800-131A with more detailed guidelines and schedules, and that NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035.

definition: NIST recommendation for stateful hash-based signature schemes LMS and XMSS, used for firmware signing and secure boot.
IETF standard defining how to use Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) for encrypted messaging.
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, requiring strong cryptography for cardholder data protection. Quantum threatens its RSA/ECC foundations.

Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a U.S. law whose Security Rule requires covered entities and business associates to protect electronic protected health information. Encryption is an addressable specification: it must be assessed and implemented where reasonable and appropriate, or the reason documented and an equivalent measure used. Patient data faces HNDL risk.
International standard series for industrial automation and control systems (IACS) cybersecurity. Critical for IoT and energy sector PQC migration.

Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts — a security framework (originally from Google) that defines increasing levels of supply chain integrity guarantees, from basic build provenance to fully hermetic, reproducible builds.
technicalNote: SLSA levels depend on cryptographic attestations signed during the build process. If those signatures use quantum-vulnerable algorithms (ECDSA, RSA), the entire SLSA guarantee collapses once quantum computers can forge attestations.

definition: An open-source framework for securing the integrity of software supply chains by defining and cryptographically verifying each step of the build and release process. Each step produces a signed attestation (a "link") forming a verifiable chain.
technicalNote: in-toto link metadata is signed with the functionary's private key. PQC migration requires upgrading all functionary keys to ML-DSA to prevent quantum forgery of supply chain attestations.

definition: NIST Special Publication providing recommendations for Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) implementation, including guidance on parameter selection and secure use of ML-KEM.
NIST Internal Report documenting the selection of HQC as an additional KEM standard, providing a code-based alternative to lattice-based ML-KEM.
IETF standard defining multiple key exchanges in IKEv2, enabling hybrid classical + PQC key exchange for IPsec VPNs.
technicalNote: Allows adding ML-KEM alongside classical Diffie-Hellman in a single IKEv2 handshake without breaking backward compatibility.

definition: IETF standard defining how to use ML-DSA digital signatures in X.509 certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs).
IETF standard defining the use of ML-DSA signatures in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), enabling PQC-signed messages and documents.
International standard for mobile driving licences (mDL), defining the data model, security mechanisms, and device engagement protocols for digital identity documents.
German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) Technical Guideline series on cryptographic recommendations, covering TLS, IPsec, SSH, and general algorithms.
technicalNote: TR-02102-1 covers general recommendations; TR-02102-2 through TR-02102-4 provide protocol-specific PQC migration guidance.

definition: NIST Special Publication 800-57: Recommendation for Key Management. Part 1 Rev. 5 (May 2020) describes four key-management phases (pre-operational, operational, post-operational and destroyed), the key states within them, and cryptoperiod guidance. Revision 6 is an initial public draft (December 2025).
A standard API (also called Cryptoki) for accessing cryptographic hardware like Hardware Security Modules (HSMs), smart cards, and tokens.
technicalNote: Defines C-language function calls for key generation, signing, encryption, and object management. PKCS#11 v3.2 adds CKM_ML_KEM_* and CKM_ML_DSA_* mechanisms for PQC.

definition: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 44, defining a multi-account hierarchy for deterministic wallets using derivation paths like m/44'/0'/0'/0/0 (purpose/coin/account/change/index).
technicalNote: Builds on BIP32 (HD wallets) and BIP43 (purpose field). Enables standard derivation paths across different cryptocurrencies and wallet implementations.

definition: NIST Special Publication defining three Deterministic Random Bit Generator (DRBG) mechanisms: CTR_DRBG (AES-based), Hash_DRBG (SHA-based), and HMAC_DRBG. Published June 2015 (Rev. 1).
technicalNote: All three DRBGs are built on symmetric primitives (hash functions, HMAC, block ciphers), which Shor's algorithm does not break; whether a given DRBG is adequate against quantum attack depends on the primitive and security strength chosen (Rev. 1 CTR_DRBG also allows three-key TDEA). That is engineering judgment, not a NIST statement. CTR_DRBG is the default in OpenSSL. Rev. 2 is not yet a draft: NIST published a pre-draft call for comments on 2025-09-04 (closed 2025-11-04) announcing plans for a new DRBG construction based on SHAKE extendable-output functions; no draft text has been published.

definition: NIST Special Publication providing methods for validating entropy sources used as input to DRBGs. Defines health tests (repetition count, adaptive proportion) and min-entropy estimation procedures. Published January 2018.
technicalNote: The NIST Entropy Source Validation (ESV) program under CMVP uses SP 800-90B to certify hardware entropy sources. The NIST EntropyAssessment tool on GitHub implements the min-entropy assessment methods.

definition: NIST Special Publication describing constructions for Random Bit Generators (RBGs) that combine entropy sources with DRBGs. Defines RBG1, RBG2, RBG3, and RBGC construction classes. Published September 2025.
technicalNote: Completes the SP 800-90 series. Specifies how to combine multiple independent entropy sources for defense-in-depth, using XOR and conditioning functions to ensure combined output retains entropy even if one source is compromised.

definition: Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR), a draft Bitcoin soft fork that adds a new native SegWit output type (version 2, bc1z… addresses) working like Taproot with the elliptic-curve key-spend path removed. It contains no post-quantum signature of its own: its authors (Hunter Beast, Ethan Heilman and Isabel Foxen Duke) intend to offer a separate proposal for that upon further research. Earlier drafts were titled P2QRH.
technicalNote: P2MR addresses use bech32m encoding (bc1z…). Every spend reveals a leaf script and a control block. The BIP says P2MR outputs are resistant to long-exposure attacks (keys exposed for longer than needed to confirm a spending transaction), and that protection against short-exposure attacks, where a key is exposed in the mempool while a transaction waits to be confirmed, may require post-quantum signatures. In the BIP's depth-1 example the P2MR witness is 135 bytes, against 66 bytes for a Taproot key-path spend.

definition: The formal proposal process for Solana protocol changes, analogous to Bitcoin BIPs and Ethereum EIPs. SIMD-0461, a proposed Falcon (FN-DSA) signature-verification syscall, was closed by its author on 2026-06-17; a commenter in the thread says Falcon-512 and Hawk-512 verifiers already work as on-chain programmes without protocol changes. HAWK has since been withdrawn from NIST's additional signatures process (29 July 2026) after a key-recovery attack.
Software Updates for Internet of Things (RFC 9019). A CBOR-based manifest format for secure firmware updates, providing metadata, conditions, and signature verification for OTA delivery.
Terminology for Constrained-Node Networks. Defines device Class 0/1/2 based on RAM and Flash memory constraints, used to categorize IoT device capabilities for protocol selection.

NIST Risk Management Framework (SP 800-37 Rev. 2) — a seven-step lifecycle process (Prepare, Categorise, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorise, Monitor) for managing information security and privacy risk in information systems and organisations.
technicalNote: The Categorise step classifies the system and its information by the impact of loss, using FIPS 199, which results in low-, moderate- or high-impact designations; the Select step then chooses and tailors control baselines. SP 800-37 Rev. 2 (December 2018) does not itself set post-quantum requirements.

definition: ISO/IEC 27005 — the international standard for information security risk management. Provides a structured methodology for identifying assets, assessing threats and vulnerabilities, evaluating risk, and selecting risk treatment options.
technicalNote: ISO 27005 uses a likelihood × consequence matrix to produce a risk level. For PQC, the threat is a CRQC; the vulnerability is use of RSA/ECC; the consequence is full plaintext exposure of harvested data. Risk treatment options: mitigate (migrate to PQC), accept, transfer, or avoid.

definition: Federal Information Processing Standard 199 — NIST's standard for categorising federal information and information systems. Defines three impact levels (Low, Moderate, High) for confidentiality, integrity, and availability that drive control selection in the NIST RMF.
technicalNote: A High rating on any one of the three objectives (confidentiality, integrity or availability) makes a federal system a high impact system. As NIST IR 8547 describes OMB M-26-15, such systems and high value assets must adopt PQC for key establishment by 31 December 2030 and for digital signatures by 31 December 2031. National security systems follow CNSA 2.0 under CNSS policy instead; M-26-15 does not apply to them.

definition: General Data Protection Regulation — EU Regulation 2016/679 requiring controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data. Article 32 lists pseudonymisation and encryption among the measures to consider, judged against the state of the art, cost and risk. The regulation names no algorithms and sets no post-quantum migration date.
technicalNote: GDPR Art. 32 ("Security of processing") requires a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking account of the state of the art, the costs of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing; encryption is listed "as appropriate". The text does not mention quantum computing. Whether long-retained personal data needs post-quantum protection is an assessment under that risk-based test (this site's reading), and how Art. 32 applies in a given case is decided by the competent supervisory authority or court.

definition: Personal Information Protection Law — China's primary data privacy law (effective November 2021), requiring data processors to adopt security measures protecting personal information. Mandates localisation of certain data and restricts cross-border transfers, making PQC migration relevant for multinational organisations with Chinese data subjects.

California Consumer Privacy Act — U.S. state law, operative since 1 January 2020 and amended by the CPRA from 1 January 2023, giving California residents rights over their personal data. Section 1798.150 lets consumers sue for statutory damages when nonencrypted and nonredacted personal information is exposed because a business failed to maintain reasonable security. The statute does not mention post-quantum cryptography.

Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados — Brazil's data protection law (Law 13.709/2018), modelled on GDPR. Article 46 requires processing agents to adopt technical and administrative security measures to protect personal data from unauthorised access and from accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration or improper processing. The national authority (ANPD) may set minimum technical standards; the law text does not mention encryption.

Personal Data Protection Act — Singapore's primary data protection law administered by the PDPC. Section 24 requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or under their control. The PDPC's guidelines say there is no one-size-fits-all solution and list encrypting personal data among example technical measures.

Digital Operational Resilience Act — EU Regulation 2022/2554, applying to financial entities and their ICT service providers from 17 January 2025. Requires an ICT risk management framework, resilience testing, and third-party risk oversight. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 requires an encryption and cryptographic-controls policy that provides for updating cryptographic technology as cryptanalysis develops; neither text sets a post-quantum migration date.
technicalNote: DORA Art. 9(4)(d) requires policies and protocols for protecting cryptographic keys, with data encrypted based on data classification and ICT risk assessment. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 Art. 6 (encryption and cryptographic controls) and Art. 7 (cryptographic key management) set the detailed policy content; its recitals refer to threats from quantum advancements, but the texts name no post-quantum algorithms.

definition: An OWASP standard for Software and Cryptography Bills of Materials (SBOM/CBOM). CycloneDX v1.6 introduced the Cryptography Asset type, enabling machine-readable inventory of all cryptographic algorithms, keys, certificates, and protocols in a system.
technicalNote: CycloneDX CBOM components include: algorithms (name, parameterSets, primitive), certificates (subject, validity, signatureAlgorithm), keys (algorithm, size), and protocols (type, version, cipher suites). Tooling: IBM Quantum Safe Explorer, Keyfactor.

definition: Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program — the NIST/CCCS program that validates implementations of Approved algorithms and their components. Testing runs black-box through NIST's ACVTS, which speaks the ACVP protocol; implementations that complete it get an algorithm validation certificate on the CAVP validation list. Algorithm validation is a prerequisite of FIPS 140-3 module validation under CMVP.
technicalNote: Source: NIST CAVP project page (csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-algorithm-validation-program): an algorithm is listed on a module certificate as an Approved security function only after it completes the algorithm validation process. ACVP sub-specifications and ACVTS testing exist for ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). Only the ACVTS production environment, used by accredited labs, creates CAVP certificates; passing public sample vectors does not.

definition: North American Electric Reliability Corporation Critical Infrastructure Protection standards. Mandatory cybersecurity requirements for bulk electric system operators.
technicalNote: CIP-012 requires an applicable Responsible Entity that owns or operates a Control Center to implement a documented plan to mitigate the risks of unauthorized disclosure and modification of real-time assessment and monitoring data sent between Control Centers; encryption is one example method, and no protocol or algorithm is named. CIP-013 requires supply chain cyber security risk management plans for high and medium impact BES Cyber Systems. Neither standard mentions post-quantum cryptography; any PQC priority for these links is analysis of a stated scenario, not a CIP requirement.

definition: International standard series for communication networks and systems in power utility automation, including substations. Its mappings cover MMS, GOOSE and Sampled Values for protection and control.
technicalNote: IEC 62351-6:2020 describes time-critical Layer 2 GOOSE and Sampled Value applications as requiring 3 ms response times and does not recommend encryption for them; authentication uses a message authentication code. Key management is specified separately in IEC 62351-9, and that public-key side is where post-quantum migration questions arise.

definition: Power systems management and associated information exchange — security standard. Covers TLS profiles, GOOSE authentication, and key management for power systems.
technicalNote: Part 3 (IEC 62351-3:2023) profiles TLS for protocols over TCP/IP; Part 4 covers profiles including MMS and derivatives (the basis for ICCP security); Part 5 (2023) secures IEC 60870-5 and derivatives, and DNP3 Secure Authentication is based on it; Part 6 (2020) secures IEC 61850 protocols including GOOSE and Sampled Values with message authentication codes; and Part 9 (2023) specifies cyber security key management. Editions differ by part, so cite the edition used.

definition: Smart Energy Profile 2.0 standard for distributed energy resource communication using certificate-based device authentication.
technicalNote: In the California Smart Inverter Profile, each communicating device has an X.509 v3 device certificate that chains to a root CA through a manufacturer CA, not a utility CA, and TLS 1.2 with TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 over P-256 is specified. A move to post-quantum certificates would need an updated profile and reissued device certificates.

definition: Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (2008). US federal law prohibiting discrimination based on genetic information in health insurance and employment. Genetic data decrypted via HNDL attacks could enable discrimination that GINA was designed to prevent.

US federal regulation providing additional privacy protections for substance use disorder patient records beyond HIPAA. Records protected under Part 2 carry heightened stigma risk if quantum-decrypted, as disclosure can lead to criminal prosecution, employment loss, and social ostracism.

FDA regulation establishing criteria for electronic records and electronic signatures in the pharmaceutical industry. Requires validated cryptographic controls for data integrity. Any PQC migration in pharma must maintain Part 11 compliance throughout the transition.
Avionics Application Standard Software Interface (ARINC 653). An RTOS partitioning standard that isolates safety-critical software functions in separate memory/time partitions on shared hardware.
technicalNote: Each ARINC 653 partition has a fixed memory budget and CPU time window. PQC libraries must fit within these constraints alongside existing avionics functions, limiting algorithm choice.

definition: Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification. The primary standard for certifying safety-critical avionics software, defining five Design Assurance Levels (DAL A through E).
technicalNote: Adding a PQC cryptographic library to a DAL-A system (e.g., Flight Management System) generally requires MC/DC structural coverage, traceability and independent verification of the changed software. Recertification cost and schedule depend on the system, the extent of the change, the certification authority and the supplier, so any published figure is an estimate for a stated project, not a value set by the standard.

definition: Airworthiness Security Process Specification. The FAA/EASA standard for addressing cybersecurity threats to airborne systems, requiring threat assessment and security controls for type certification.
technicalNote: DO-326A mandates that cryptographic protections be evaluated against evolving threats including quantum computing. Aircraft manufacturers must demonstrate PQC readiness as part of the airworthiness security risk assessment.

definition: US export control regulations (22 CFR 120-130) governing the export and transfer of defense articles and services, including military cryptographic systems listed on the US Munitions List.
technicalNote: ITAR Category XI covers military cryptographic equipment. PQC implementations for military aircraft or defense satellites require State Department export licenses. No license exceptions exist for embargoed destinations.

definition: A technical standard by the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity that embeds cryptographically signed metadata into digital content to verify its origin, creation method, and edit history.
technicalNote: C2PA signs the claim in each manifest with a COSE_Sign1 signature and X.509 certificate chains to create tamper-evident provenance chains. C2PA 2.4 allows ECDSA, RSASSA-PSS and Ed25519 signatures, all quantum-vulnerable, and its allowed list holds no post-quantum algorithm, so moving to ML-DSA signatures would take a revision of the specification. Provenance signed today stays forgeable beyond Q-Day.

definition: Automotive Safety Integrity Level, a risk classification defined by ISO 26262: ASIL A (lowest) to ASIL D (highest integrity requirements), plus QM (quality management, no safety requirement). The level comes from a hazard analysis of severity, exposure and controllability, and sets how rigorous the safety measures must be.
technicalNote: The ASIL label does not by itself fix a cryptographic latency budget, redundancy scheme or fail-operational behaviour. Such requirements are derived for each item from its hazard analysis and its fault tolerant time interval (FTTI), the time a fault can be present before a hazardous event; checks must fit inside that budget on the target hardware. The safe reaction to a failed or late verification is decided in the item's safety concept. Any specific figure, such as a millisecond verification budget or a dual PQC and classical path, is a design assumption for a stated scenario and should be labelled as one.

definition: Trusted Information Security Assessment Exchange, a standard for information security assessments in the automotive supply chain governed by VDA (German Association of the Automotive Industry) and ENX.
technicalNote: TISAX v7 (expected 2027) is anticipated to add PQC readiness criteria. OEMs requiring TISAX compliance from Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers will cascade PQC requirements through the supply chain. Assessment scope will likely cover key management, firmware signing, and cryptographic inventory.

definition: AUTomotive Open System ARchitecture, a standardized software architecture for automotive ECUs, with a Classic Platform and an Adaptive Platform. On the Classic Platform, software calls the Crypto Service Manager (CSM), which reaches software or hardware crypto drivers (for example an HSM or SHE) through the Crypto Interface. On the Adaptive Platform, the Cryptography functional cluster exposes the ara::crypto API, with crypto providers behind it.
technicalNote: The two platforms specify different crypto interfaces, so Classic and Adaptive software are not interchangeable. In release R25-11, the Adaptive Cryptography specification lists algorithm identifiers for ML-DSA, ML-KEM and SLH-DSA, while the Classic CSM, Crypto Interface and Crypto Driver specifications list algorithm families such as AES, RSA and ECDSA plus a custom family and do not mention post-quantum algorithms. Whether a given ECU can run a post-quantum algorithm depends on its crypto driver or provider, memory, processing power and any hardware security module, so it has to be assessed per ECU.

definition: An international standard for vehicle-to-grid communication enabling Plug & Charge: automatic mutual authentication between electric vehicles and charging stations using X.509 certificates over TLS.
technicalNote: ISO 15118 uses a PKI hierarchy (OEM Root CA → Vehicle Sub-CA → Vehicle Leaf Cert) with ECDSA P-256. PQC migration requires updating the entire Plug & Charge PKI to hybrid certificates, affecting vehicle OEMs, Charge Point Operators (CPOs), and eMobility Service Providers (eMSPs).

definition: The security standard for Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments (WAVE), defining V2X message signing, certificate formats, and the Security Credential Management System (SCMS) for pseudonym certificate issuance.
technicalNote: IEEE 1609.2 currently mandates ECDSA P-256 for V2X message signing and ECIES for encryption. A PQC amendment (expected 2025-2026) will add ML-DSA and ML-KEM support. The SCMS uses butterfly key expansion to generate millions of unlinkable pseudonym certificates — this mechanism must be adapted for PQC key sizes.

definition: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program — a U.S. government-wide program that provides a standardized approach to security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring for cloud products and services used by federal agencies.
technicalNote: Under FedRAMP's Consolidated Rules for 2026, the use of cryptographic modules validated by the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program depends on the certification class: Class A and B providers may use them, Class C providers should and Class D providers must. OMB M-26-15 tells agencies to engage their FedRAMP-authorized cloud providers about PQC migration responsibilities. CNSA 2.0 dates apply to national security systems, not to FedRAMP.

definition: Common Criteria scoring scale from EAL1 (lowest) to EAL7 (highest) that grades the depth and rigor of a product's security evaluation. Higher EAL means more design analysis, more testing, and stronger evidence requirements — not necessarily a more secure product.

NIST CSWP 39 — Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility: Strategies and Practices (Update 1; first published December 19, 2025, updated June 29, 2026). Covers crypto agility in security protocols and in system implementations, a strategic plan for managing an organization's cryptographic risks, and an illustrative four-tier maturity model adapted from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework tiers (Partial → Risk-Informed → Repeatable → Adaptive). The five-pillar model used in PQC Today's Crypto Management module (inventory, governance, lifecycle, observability, assurance) is this site's own teaching overlay, not a NIST taxonomy.

EU directive (2022/2555) requiring enhanced cybersecurity controls across critical-infrastructure sectors. Transposition deadline October 2024; enforcement ongoing across member states. Mandates appropriate cryptographic measures without naming PQC explicitly.

acronym: electronic IDentification, Authentication and trust Services
definition: EU regulation (No 910/2014) governing electronic identification and trust services across member states. Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2.0) establishes the European Digital Identity Framework: each Member State must provide at least one European Digital Identity Wallet within 24 months of the entry into force of the implementing acts. The amending text sets no post-quantum requirements.

EU regulation (2024/2847) imposing cybersecurity requirements on products with digital elements. Entered force December 2024; full obligations apply 11 December 2027 (reporting obligations from September 2026).

AICPA audit framework evaluating a service provider's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Cryptographic-control adequacy is evaluated within the security criterion.

International standard specifying requirements for an Information Security Management System (ISMS). Annex A.10 covers cryptography. Does not mandate PQC directly but the control framework drives PQC adoption.

DISA-maintained configuration standards that lock down DoD information systems and components. STIGs prescribe specific cryptographic-suite choices, with ongoing updates to reflect CNSA 2.0 / FIPS 140-3 alignment.

acronym: Certification de Sécurité de Premier Niveau
definition: ANSSI's first-level security certification scheme for IT products. Faster and lighter than full Common Criteria; PQC products began entering CSPN catalogue in 2025.

NIST Internal Report (October 2024) that down-selected the PQC signature on-ramp to 14 second-round candidates across four mathematical families: MPC-in-the-Head, multivariate, isogeny, and lattice. Superseded by NIST IR 8610 (May 2026), which closed the second round and advanced nine candidates to the third round.

CA/Browser Forum ballot (April 2025) that phases TLS certificate maximum validity from 398 days down to 200d (2026), 100d (2027), and 47d by March 2029. Forces every public-trust TLS deployment onto automated CLM.

US Office of Management and Budget memorandum (November 2022) directing federal agencies to submit an annual prioritized inventory of quantum-vulnerable cryptographic systems (excluding national security systems) until 2035 or as superseding guidance directs, plus an assessment of the funding needed to migrate them.
technicalNote: OMB M-23-02 sets the recurring inventory cadence for non-national-security federal systems, with a focus on high value assets and high impact systems. OMB M-26-15 (June 2026) later requires agencies to submit PQC Migration Plans and sets migration phases. National security systems are outside both memoranda and follow CNSA 2.0 under NSS policy.

definition: National Security Memorandum on Promoting United States Leadership in Quantum Computing While Mitigating Risks to Vulnerable Cryptographic Systems, signed May 4, 2022. Directs NSA, CISA, and NIST to inventory cryptographic systems and sets migration timelines for National Security Systems.
technicalNote: Implemented via OMB Memorandum M-23-02, which required agencies to submit cryptographic inventories.

definition: The predecessor to FIPS 140-3 for validating cryptographic modules. NIST's CMVP stopped accepting new FIPS 140-2 submissions in 2021; many previously validated modules remain listed during a multi-year transition to FIPS 140-3.
NSA's original Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite (2015), specifying classical algorithms — RSA-3072, ECDH/ECDSA P-384, SHA-384, AES-256 — for protecting National Security Systems.
technicalNote: Superseded by CNSA 2.0 (2022, already in this glossary), which adds PQC algorithms and sets adoption timelines.

definition: Recommendation for Pair-Wise Key-Establishment Using Discrete Logarithm Cryptography — the NIST standard specifying Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve (ECDH) key-agreement schemes.
Recommendation for Pair-Wise Key-Establishment Using Integer Factorization Cryptography — the NIST standard specifying RSA-based key-transport and key-agreement schemes.

Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes — the NIST standard specifying the two-step (extract-then-expand) key-derivation approach used to turn a shared secret from SP 800-56A/B, or a PQC KEM, into usable keying material.

Recommendation for Discrete Logarithm-based Cryptography: Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters — the NIST standard specifying the NIST curves (P-256, P-384, P-521) used throughout TLS, X.509, and other classical or hybrid cryptography.
The IETF specification for XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme) and XMSS^MT, the stateful hash-based signature schemes also standardized by NIST SP 800-208.
The IETF specification for LMS (Leighton-Micali Signatures) and its multi-tree variant HSS, the stateful hash-based signature schemes also standardized by NIST SP 800-208.
Report on Post-Quantum Cryptography (April 2016) — NIST's original report announcing the PQC standardization project and surveying the state of quantum-resistant cryptography at the time.

Status Report on the Second Round of the NIST PQC Standardization Process (July 2020), narrowing the KEM and signature candidates to the finalists and alternates that became ML-KEM, ML-DSA, FN-DSA, and SLH-DSA.

Status Report on the Third Round of the NIST PQC Standardization Process (July 2022), announcing the selection of ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and FN-DSA for standardization and continued fourth-round evaluation of alternate KEMs (BIKE, Classic McEliece, HQC, SIKE).
technicalNote: SIKE was withdrawn after a 2022 cryptanalytic break; HQC was later selected via NIST IR 8545, already in this glossary.

definition: The RSA Cryptography Standard, specifying RSA encryption and signature padding schemes (PKCS#1 v1.5, OAEP, PSS) used across TLS, S/MIME, and code signing.
The Cryptographic Message Syntax standard for signing and encrypting arbitrary data, superseded by and largely synonymous with IETF CMS — the basis for S/MIME and code-signing signature formats.
The standard syntax for encoding a private key, optionally password-encrypted, independent of its algorithm — the format OpenSSL's genpkey produces for RSA, ECDSA, and PQC key types alike.
